etymology: Hebrew ‘azmaveth, “strong as death” or “strength of death,” a town of Benjamin, also called Beth-azmaveth, whose men returned from the captivity in Babylon.
biblical_def: Azmaveth is the name of a small town of Benjamin, reckoned in the lists of those who came up out of the captivity of Babylon with Zerubbabel, when the LORD stirred the spirit of His remnant to return and rebuild (Ezr 2:24). It is called Beth-azmaveth, “the house of Azmaveth,” in the parallel register that Nehemiah preserved, where two and forty of its men are numbered (Neh 7:28), and its singers were gathered to the dedication of the wall (Neh 12:29). The name itself, “strong as death,” sits strangely upon a place so easily passed over, yet the strength here is not of the town but of the God who brought its handful of men home over the long road from Babylon. The dictionary does not feign a history for Azmaveth where Scripture is silent; it honours that the Spirit of God thought it good to count even these few souls in the book of the return. For the LORD had said by Cyrus, Who is there among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up; and the men of Azmaveth went up. Azmaveth stands as a witness that the providence of God numbers the least of His returning remnant, that not one town and not one family of His people should be lost, but all be gathered to rebuild the house and the worship of the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew geba‘, “hill” or “height,” a city of Benjamin given to the priests, whose men returned from the captivity in Babylon.
biblical_def: Geba was a city of the tribe of Benjamin, given with its suburbs to the priests, the sons of Aaron, when the land was parted by lot under Joshua (Jos 21:17). It lay on the northern border of Judah, so that the bounds of the kingdom were spoken of as from Geba to Beersheba, and it is named among the towns whose men came up out of Babylon with Zerubbabel, six hundred twenty and one of them (Ezr 2:26; Neh 7:30). After the wall was built, the children of Benjamin dwelt again at Geba and the towns round about (Neh 11:31). The name signifies “hill” or “height,” and the dictionary is careful to mark Geba as distinct from Gibeah and Gibeon, with which the unwary reader may confound it. What it honours is that this priestly town was not left desolate, but its sons returned to dwell where their fathers had dwelt and to serve at the altar that should be rebuilt. For the LORD had not cast off His priesthood, but kept a seed of them through the captivity, and stirred their spirit to go up. Geba stands as a witness that the providence of God restores His ministers to their places, that the priestly cities should be filled again, and that the worship of His house should not fail but be re-established by the remnant He brought home.

etymology: Hebrew nebo, a name of uncertain meaning, perhaps “height,” here a town of Judah or Benjamin whose men returned from the captivity in Babylon.
biblical_def: Nebo, in this place, is the name of a small town whose men, two and fifty of them, are numbered among those who returned from the captivity of Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:29; Neh 7:33). It is carefully to be distinguished from Mount Nebo in the land of Moab, that height of Pisgah whither Moses went up to behold the promised land before he died and was buried by the hand of the LORD; and from Nebo the idol of Babylon, that bowed and stooped with Bel when the LORD brought down the gods of the captors. The dictionary marks these apart, that the reader confound not the town of the returnees with the mountain of Moses’ death nor with the heathen god. Of this Nebo the Scripture records only the number of its men in the book of the return, yet that is no small honour, for they were among the remnant whose spirit God had raised to go up and rebuild. The men of Nebo are named again among those who had taken strange wives and put them away in the days of Ezra’s reformation (Ezr 10:43). Nebo stands as a witness that the providence of God numbered even this little company in the great gathering home, and that the LORD, who buries His servant Moses and casts down the idols of Babylon, loses not the least of His returning people.

etymology: Hebrew magbish, perhaps “congregating” or “gathering,” a town or company of Judah whose men returned from the captivity in Babylon.
biblical_def: Magbish is named but once in all the Scripture, in the register of those who came up out of the captivity of Babylon, where an hundred fifty and six of its children are numbered among the remnant of Zerubbabel’s company (Ezr 2:30). Whether it was a town of Judah or a family reckoned by their head, the dictionary will not feign to know where the LORD was pleased to record only the name and the number; yet the name itself, perhaps signifying “gathering,” falls fitly upon a people gathered home from a far land. For this was the great work of that hour, that the LORD, having sent His people into Babylon for their sins, should turn again their captivity and gather them by the proclamation of Cyrus, whose spirit He had stirred. The men of Magbish are not named in Nehemiah’s parallel list, so that this once-spoken name might easily have perished from memory; but the Spirit of God set it down, that not one company of the returning should be unremembered. Magbish stands as a witness that the providence of God gathers His scattered people one band at a time, and counts each into His book; and it points beyond itself to the great gathering, when the Lord shall gather together His elect from the four winds, and not one of all whom the Father hath given Him shall be lost.

etymology: Hebrew charim, “consecrated” or “devoted,” the name of a company of the people, three hundred and twenty of whose men returned from the captivity in Babylon.
biblical_def: Harim, in this place, names a company of the people, three hundred and twenty of whose men are numbered among those who came up out of the captivity of Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:32; Neh 7:35). It is carefully to be distinguished from Harim the priestly course, the third of the four and twenty orders into which David parted the sons of Aaron, of whom a thousand and seventeen returned, and from Harim a family of priests and one of the layfolk that signed the covenant in the days of Nehemiah. The name signifies “consecrated” or “devoted,” from the root of that which is set apart wholly unto the LORD. The dictionary marks these Harims apart, that the reader confound not the lay company of the return with the priestly course of the same name. Of this company of the people the Scripture records the number of its men in the book of the return, and that some of them too were found among those who had taken strange wives and put them away. Harim stands as a witness that the LORD numbered His common people, no less than His priests, in the great return; that the consecration signified by the name belongs to the whole congregation of the redeemed, who are called a holy nation, a peculiar people, set apart to show forth the praises of Him who hath called them out of darkness into His marvellous light.

etymology: Hebrew senaah, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “thorny” or “the hated,” a company also called Hassenaah, whose children returned from Babylon and built the fish gate of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Senaah, called also Hassenaah, names a company of the people whose children, a great number, three thousand six hundred and thirty, are reckoned among those who returned from the captivity of Babylon (Ezr 2:35; Neh 7:38). Though the name may signify “the hated,” the LORD set no contempt upon these returning sons, but gave them a labour of honour; for the sons of Hassenaah built the fish gate, laying the beams thereof and setting up its doors, its locks, and its bars, in the rebuilding of the wall under Nehemiah (Neh 3:3). The dictionary honours that a company so numerous, whose very name might be read as a reproach, was found foremost at the wall, building one of its gates with their own hands. For the fish gate was no small charge, but a true breach to be repaired and shut against the enemy. There is gospel here, that the LORD takes a people who might be called the hated and makes them builders of His city; for He hath said of His church, In the place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, there shall they be called the children of the living God. Senaah stands as a witness that the providence of God turns reproach into honour, and sets the lowly and the despised to build the walls of His Jerusalem.

etymology: Hebrew ‘anathoth, perhaps “answers” or “answered prayers,” a priestly city of Benjamin, the home of Jeremiah, whose men returned from the captivity in Babylon.
biblical_def: Anathoth was a city of Benjamin given with its suburbs to the priests, the sons of Aaron, in the parting of the land under Joshua (Jos 21:18); and it was the home of Jeremiah the prophet, who was of the priests that were in Anathoth (Jer 1:1). An hundred twenty and eight of its men are numbered among those who returned from the captivity of Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:23; Neh 7:27). The name, which some read as “answers” or “answered prayers,” carries a weight of mercy, for it was at Anathoth that the LORD bade Jeremiah, in the very hour of the siege, to buy the field of his uncle’s son, a sign that houses and fields and vineyards should yet be possessed again in the land. The dictionary marks this town of Anathoth, where the weeping prophet was born, as distinct from the bare mention of the name elsewhere. What it honours is that the very town from which Jeremiah cried God’s word of judgment and of hope was not left desolate, but its priestly sons came home, an answer to the promise the prophet had bought with seventeen shekels of silver. Anathoth stands as a witness that the LORD performs His word; that the city of the prophet of the captivity should be the city of the returning remnant; and that the God who answers prayer brings His people back to the fields their fathers tilled.

etymology: From the Babylonian, perhaps “may Shamash protect the father” or “worshipper of fire,” the name given to a prince of Judah who brought back the vessels of the house of the LORD from Babylon.
biblical_def: Sheshbazzar is called the prince of Judah, into whose hand Cyrus the king delivered the vessels of the house of the LORD which Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem and put in the house of his gods (Ezr 1:8). When the captivity was turned, Cyrus numbered out these holy vessels, the chargers and the basons and the bowls, and committed all to Sheshbazzar to be brought up with the returning remnant unto Jerusalem (Ezr 1:11). And it was this same Sheshbazzar who, by the king’s decree, came and laid the foundation of the house of God which is in Jerusalem, as the elders testified before Darius (Ezr 5:14-16). His name is of Babylon, given as Daniel was named Belteshazzar, yet the man bore a Hebrew heart, a prince of the captivity entrusted with the sacred things. The dictionary honours that the LORD raised up a leader to carry home the vessels of His worship and to lay again the temple’s foundation, the first stone of the long work that Zerubbabel and Jeshua should carry on. There is mercy here, that the holy things plundered in judgment were not lost but restored; for the LORD will not suffer His worship to perish. Sheshbazzar stands as a witness that the providence of God preserves the means of His worship through the captivity, and raises up His servants to begin the rebuilding of His house.

He who kept the vessels of His house safe in Babylon, and committed them to Sheshbazzar to bring home, is the same who will not suffer His worship to fail. The saint who fears the cause of God may be overthrown by the powers of the earth may remember Sheshbazzar, bearing the holy things back to Zion, and laying again the foundation of the LORD’s house.
roots_summary: From a Babylonian name, Sheshbazzar marks the prince of Judah who brought the temple vessels home.
roots_lines: Sheshbazzar — from the Babylonian, perhaps “may Shamash protect the father.”
He is called the prince of Judah at the return from Babylon.
Cyrus delivered into his hand the vessels of the house of the LORD.
He brought the holy vessels up unto Jerusalem with the captivity.
He laid the foundation of the house of God by the king’s decree.
usage: Like Sheshbazzar bearing home the vessels, the LORD preserves the means of His worship through every judgment.
The God who kept the holy things in Babylon raised up a prince to carry them back and lay the temple’s foundation.
The cause of God is never overthrown, but its first foundation is laid again by the servants He appoints.

etymology: Hebrew yeshua‘, “the LORD is salvation,” a form of the name Joshua and of Jesus, borne by Jeshua the son of Jozadak, high priest of the return.
biblical_def: Jeshua the son of Jozadak was the high priest of the return from Babylon, who with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel rose up and built the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon as it is written in the law of Moses (Ezr 3:2). In the second year of their coming, he with Zerubbabel set forward the work of the house of the LORD (Ezr 3:8), and when the building was hindered, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah stirred them up, and Jeshua rose again to build (Ezr 5:2; Hag 1:1). Zechariah saw him in vision standing before the angel of the LORD, clothed with filthy garments, and Satan at his right hand to resist him; and the LORD rebuked Satan, took away his filthy garments, and clothed him with change of raiment, a figure of the cleansing of the priesthood by grace alone (Zec 3:1-9). The dictionary is careful to distinguish this man Jeshua, son of Jozadak, from the village of Jeshua in the south of Judah named in the same records. His very name, “the LORD is salvation,” is the name of Jesus our great High Priest; and Zechariah’s vision points beyond Jeshua to the Branch, the LORD’s servant, who should remove iniquity in one day. Jeshua stands as a witness that the LORD restores His priesthood, clothing the unworthy in His own righteousness, and that the high priest of the return foreshadows the High Priest of our profession, Christ Jesus.
webster_summary: Jeshua the son of Jozadak, high priest of the return, who built the altar and labored with Zerubbabel.
webster_full: JESHUA, the son of Jozadak, high priest at the return from Babylon.
With Zerubbabel he built the altar and offered burnt offerings as Moses commanded.
He set forward the work of the house of the LORD in the second year.
Zechariah saw him cleansed of filthy garments by the grace of God.
His name “the LORD is salvation” is the very name of Jesus our High Priest.
scriptures: Ezr 3:2

Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as it is written in the law of Moses the man of God.
Zec 3:4

And he answered and spake unto those that stood before him, saying, Take away the filthy garments from him. And unto him he said, Behold, I have caused thine iniquity to pass from thee, and I will clothe thee with change of raiment.
Ezr 5:2
Then rose up Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and began to build the house of God which is at Jerusalem: and with them were the prophets of God helping them.
Hag 1:1

In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet unto Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Josedech, the high priest, saying,
corruption_summary: A man of Scripture, not a contested doctrine; he witnesses to the LORD’s restoring of His priesthood and foreshadows Christ our High Priest.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeshua the son of Jozadak is a man of the sacred record, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine him. The dictionary records him, and distinguishes him from the village of Jeshua in Judah, that the reader who meets the name may know him for a real high priest, raised up by a real God to restore the altar and the worship of His house.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the cleansing and restoring of the priesthood by grace alone, and its fulfilment in Christ. He who took away the filthy garments of Jeshua and clothed him with change of raiment is the same who clothes His people in the righteousness of His Son. The saint who feels the filthiness of his own garments may remember Jeshua before the angel, and look to Jesus, whose very name Jeshua bore, the great High Priest who removes iniquity in one day.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the LORD is salvation,” Jeshua names the high priest of the return, a figure of Christ.
roots_lines: Jeshua — Hebrew yeshua‘, “the LORD is salvation.”
It is a form of the name Joshua and of Jesus.
Jeshua the son of Jozadak was high priest at the return.
He built the altar and labored with Zerubbabel on the house of the LORD.
He must be distinguished from the village of Jeshua in Judah.
usage: Like Jeshua cleansed of his filthy garments, the believer is clothed by grace in the righteousness of Christ.
The LORD who restored His high priest at the return raised up Jesus, whose name Jeshua bore, the great High Priest.
The God who built again His altar by Jeshua’s hand restores the worship of His house in every age.

etymology: Hebrew elyashib, “God restores” or “whom God restores,” the high priest in Nehemiah’s day who built the sheep gate but compromised by lodging Tobiah in the temple courts.
biblical_def: Eliashib was the high priest in the days of Nehemiah, who with his brethren the priests rose up and built the sheep gate, sanctified it, and set up its doors, leading the great work of rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem (Neh 3:1). To begin the labour, and at the holy gate by which the sacrifices entered, was honour indeed. Yet the same Eliashib, being allied unto Tobiah the Ammonite, that enemy of God’s people who had mocked and resisted the building, prepared for him a great chamber in the courts of the house of God, in the very place where the offerings and the tithes had been laid up (Neh 13:4-5). When Nehemiah returned and learned of the evil, he cast forth all Tobiah’s household stuff out of the chamber and cleansed it (Neh 13:7-9,28). The dictionary honours the building of the sheep gate but will not hide the compromise, for here is a sober warning of the unequal yoke. The high priest, whose name means “God restores,” gave a chamber in the temple to the very foe of the temple, mingling the holy with the profane through alliance with the ungodly. Eliashib stands as a witness that a man may begin a good work and yet corrupt it by friendship with the enemies of God; and he calls every steward of holy things to be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers, lest the courts of the LORD be defiled.
webster_summary: The high priest in Nehemiah’s day who built the sheep gate but lodged Tobiah the Ammonite in the temple courts.
webster_full: ELIASHIB, the high priest in the days of Nehemiah, signifying “God restores.”
He with the priests built the sheep gate and sanctified it.
Being allied to Tobiah the Ammonite, he gave him a chamber in the temple courts.
Nehemiah cast out Tobiah’s stuff and cleansed the chamber on his return.
It witnesses both to good labour begun and to the corruption of an unequal yoke.
scriptures: Neh 3:1

Then Eliashib the high priest rose up with his brethren the priests, and they builded the sheep gate; they sanctified it, and set up the doors of it; even unto the tower of Meah they sanctified it, unto the tower of Hananeel.
Neh 13:7
And I came to Jerusalem, and understood of the evil that Eliashib did for Tobiah, in preparing him a chamber in the courts of the house of God.
Neh 13:9
Then I commanded, and they cleansed the chambers: and thither brought I again the vessels of the house of God, with the meat offering and the frankincense.
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
corruption_summary: His building was good, but Eliashib’s alliance with Tobiah is a true warning against the unequal yoke that defiles the house of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Eliashib the high priest is honoured for rising up to build the sheep gate, the first labour named in the rebuilding of the wall; and the dictionary will not strip him of that honour. Yet his is not the caveat of an obscure name untouched by controversy, for the Scripture itself names his fault, that the reader may learn from it. The high priest who began the wall ended by giving the enemy of the wall a room within the holy courts.

The corruption to avoid is the unequal yoke that mingles the holy with the profane. Eliashib, whose name means “God restores,” was allied unto Tobiah the Ammonite, the very man who had laughed the builders to scorn, and lodged him where the tithes of the LORD had been stored. So a good work was defiled by friendship with the ungodly, until Nehemiah cast the stuff forth and cleansed the place. The LORD warns every steward of His house: be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers, for the courts of God are not to be let out to His enemies, and the church that befriends the world betrays the trust of her Lord.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “God restores,” Eliashib names the high priest who built the sheep gate but compromised with Tobiah.
roots_lines: Eliashib — Hebrew elyashib, “God restores” or “whom God restores.”
He was the high priest in the days of Nehemiah.
He with the priests built and sanctified the sheep gate.
He gave Tobiah the Ammonite a chamber in the courts of the house of God.
His grandson married the daughter of Sanballat and was chased away by Nehemiah.
usage: Like Eliashib, a man may begin a good work and yet defile it by friendship with the enemies of God.
The sheep gate well built cannot excuse a chamber given to Tobiah in the courts of the LORD.
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers, lest the holy house be let out to its foes.
